note: Absolute budgets, deliberately loose: they exist to catch a large regression, not a 5% one.
Bytes are content, so they are machine-independent and can be tight. Timings are not, so their
headroom is ~3x (char) to ~5x (line) over the laptop they were set from: they trip at a ~4x
regression there. A machine N times slower multiplies its timing budgets by N
(KRD_BENCH_BUDGET_SCALE, 7.6 in CI) instead of these numbers being widened for everyone.
docs/BENCHMARK.md section 6 has the measurement, how to re-run it, and why a single absolute
number cannot also be a 2x gate on a 7.6x-slower runner.
photo bytes.wire (15,000,000) is ~10% over today's 13,580,155 on the pinned layout -- the same
'catch a large regression, not a 5% one' rule as the rest of this file, deliberately not a tight
ratchet: photo is deterministic noise, so 0.9% would be exactly reproducible, but it would fire
on any framing/tile change and invite someone to widen it silently, which is how budgets rot.
The number to ratchet down when a fix lands is in docs/research-photo-bandwidth.md.
photoReal (5.6 MB payload on the pinned layout) is the photographic counterpart of photo:
low-frequency structure plus grain, deterministic integer content, lossless ratio ~0.5. Its
budget is set the same way -- ~1.5x the measurement, i.e. it fires on a large regression, not
on a few percent. Do not ratchet it to the measured number: the point of the case is to stay
comparable when the encoder changes.
Every budget here is measured at --scale 1 (the default). --scale 0.5 captures a quarter of the
pixels and cuts photo wire to 3.4 MB, so it is a deliberate way to go under these numbers, not a
way to pass them: a run that changes the scale must say so next to its result.
